div.p: This paper presents a new algorithm for the on-line scheduling of hard deadline aperiodic tasks in a realtime system in which hard deadline periodic tasks are scheduled using a fized priority algorithm. The algorithm for jointly scheduling the periodic and aperiodic tasks eztends the slack stealing algorithm introduced by Lehoczky and Ramos-Thuel, and thus provides the largest amount of time for aperiodic task processing subject to meeting all periodic task deadlines. The analysis permits the periodic tasks to consist of a set of serially executed subtasks each of which has its own fized ezecution priority as defined by Gonzalez Harbour et. al.. Thus the model permits ihe direct inclusion of operating system functions as well as certain types of synchronization protocols directly into ihe schedulability analysis. The methods provide a unified framework for dealing with several related problems including: reclaiming unused periodic and aperiodic execution time, load shedding, balancing hard and soft aperiodic ezecution time and coping with transient overloads.'

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In the last several years, fixed priority scheduling algorithms have gained popularity as a method for designing predictable real-time systems, especially because these scheduling algorithms have been developed to permit the solution of many practical problems such as transient overload, task synchronization and the joint scheduling of periodic and aperiodic tasks. The analysis techniques have been broadened to include factors such as operating system functions [l] and precedence constraints within the task set [2].

In this paper, we consider the problem of jointly scheduling hard deadline periodic tasks and hard deadline aperiodic tasks. The methods we present are an extension of the slack stealing algorithm introduced by Lehoczky and Ramos-Thuel [3]. This fixed priority algorithm was designed to service soft deadline aperiodic tasks while guaranteeing the hard deadlines of periodic tasks. It was proved to be optimal in the sense that it simultaneously minimized the response time of all aperiodic tasks, provided they were served in FIFO order. Our method in this paper is based on the use of the slack stealing algorithm, which provides the maximum amount of processing capacity for aperiodic tasks, while still guaranteeing the deadlines of the periodic tasks. There is, however, an important difference between the soft and hard deadline aperiodic cases. All soft deadline tasks will eventually be completed; however, some hard deadline tasks cannot be accepted for processing because they cannot meet their deadline.

Work on the on-line scheduling of hard aperiodic tasks has been recently reported by Chetto and Chetto [4] and Schwan and Zhou [5]. Their work assumes that periodic tasks are scheduled according to the Earliest Deadline algorithm, which assigns priorities to tasks dynamically with the task having the nearest deadline receiving the highest priority. The Earliest Deadline algorithm was proved to be the optimal preemptive scheduling algorithm for scheduling hard periodic tasks in dynamic priority systems [6].

Chetto and Chetto proposed an algorithm which determines the location and duration of processor idle times for any arbitrary window of time. This a l p rithm was designed to schedule hard aperiodic tasks. The computational complexity of allocating time for the service of an aperiodic request and the execution of its acceptance test is O(n), where n is the number of periodic tasks. Chetto and Chetto's algorithm has certain shortcomings. First, the timing correctness of the algorithm requires that the periodic tasks be initiated at a critical instant and that periodic task deadlines be equal to their periods. Second, the algorithm as- sumes that when any hard aperiodic task arrives and is required to run, all the aperiodic tasks previously accepted have completed their execution.

Schwan and Zhou relax the assumptions made by Chetto and Chetto. They propose an elegant and simple joint scheduling algorithm that can schedule a task with a worst-case time complexity of O(nlogn). Unlike Chetto and Chetto's algorithm, Schwan and Zhou's algorithm does not give preferential treatment to the periodic tasks. Every task, whether periodic or aperiodic, is subject to an acceptance test upon arrival. Unfortunately, this results in undesirable implementation overheads if the real-time workload is mainly periodic.

We adopt a fixed priority approach to the joint scheduling problem, thus each periodic task must receive a fixed priority. We assume that priorities are assigned by the Deadline Monotonic algorithm [7]. We also assume that each hard aperiodic task is assigned a fixed priority, but different aperiodics may receive different priorities. While the fixed priority approach has the drawbacks of achieving a lower level of schedulability for the periodic tasks and offering lower envelopes on the amount of computation time that may be devoted to aperiodics over any window, there are several advantages. First, many existing systems are based on fixed priority scheduling because of its simplicity and ability to handle many practical problems. Second, we present our analysis using a more general periodic task model, namely the model introduced by Gonzalez Harbour et. al. [2]. In this model, each task is composed of subtasks which are executed serially, and each can have a different execution priority. The advantage of this model is that one can incorporate certain types of precedence constraints among the tasks, can include non-preemptable sections, operating system functions and certain task synchronization protocols. Thus, the hard aperiodic scheduling problem is being addressed for the first time for fixed priority systems in a fairly general and useful context. This paper is organized as follows. In sections 2 and 3, we present the model, notation and the slack stealing computations. Section 4 addresses the question of the optimality of any algorithm, then presents the slack stealing algorithm for hard aperiodic tasks. Section 5 discusses the implementation requirements of the slack stealing approach. Finally, we note that the slack stealing approach offers a unified framework for dealing with several related problems including: reclaiming unused periodic and aperiodic execution times, load shedding, balancing hard and soft aperiodic execution time and coping with transient overloads. These generalizations are discussed in section 6. Section 7 concludes the paper.

div.head: Task Execution Model
div.p: Consider a real-time system with n periodic tasks, T I , . . ., 7,. Each task, ri, has a worst-case computation requirement Ci, a period Ti, an initiation time or offset relative to some time origin 6; 2 0, and a hard deadline di. Each periodic task is composed of distinct subtasks which are executed serially. Thus, ri consists of m(i) subtasks, r / , . . . , T,?(~). Each subtask is characterized by a worst case computation time, C!, and an execution priority, P!. We assume C: +. , . +C,y(i) = Ci. The parameters C!, Ti, q$, and di are known deterministic quantities. We require that these tasks be scheduled according to a fixed priority algorithm in that each subtask is assigned a fixed execution priority Pi'. We want the priority assignment to closely approximate the deadline monotonic priority assignment in which tasks with small values of di are given relatively high priority. This priority assignment was proved to be optimal for the special case in which di 5 Ti [7]; however, we do not require this condition to hold. Most subtasks of each of the periodic tasks will be assigned the deadline monotonic execution priority associated with the task, Pi. We assume that the periodic tasks are indexed in priority order with TI having highest priority and T, having lowest priority, that is dl 5 dz 5 . . . 5 d,. For simplicity, we set Pi = i , with 1 indicating highest priority and n the lowest among the periodic tasks. Some subtasks may receive an elevated execution priority, for example to enforce non-preemptability during synchronization or during the execution ,of an operating system function. Thus we assume Pi' 5 i , where smaller priority values indicate higher execution priorities. For example, if a part of the task were to be run non-preemptively, say to enforce mutual exclusion on a shared data object, we could let that part of the task be a subtask with an execution priority higher than level 1. This would ensure that it could be interrupted only by operating system functions. One can also model more sophisticated task synchronization protocols such as priority ceiling protocol emulation [SI. In this protocol, a subtask is assigned an execution priority equal to the highest priority of any task that shares the data object.

A periodic task, say ri, gives rise to an infinite sequence of jobs. The kth such job, r i k , is ready at time 4i + ( k -1 ) r and its Ci units of required execution must be completed by time di + ( k -1 ) r + di or else a periodic task timing fault will occur.

We next introduce the aperiodic tasks, { J k , k 2 1). Each aperiodic job, Jk, has an associated arrival time a k , a processing requirement p k , and a hard deadline, Dk. The tasks are indexed such that 0 5 a k 5 (Yk+l,k 2 1. w e assume that the aperiodic task sequence is not known in advance; however, when an aperiodic task arrives, its worst case computation requirement and deadline are known. When an aperiodic task arrives, an acceptance test is performed to determine whether the task can meet its deadline without causing any of the periodic tasks to miss their deadlines. An accepted task is enqueued in deadline order within the assigned execution priority level. The acceptance test is run immediately, and any aperiodic task that fails the test is immediately discarded. There are a number of different possible approaches to deciding which aperiodic tasks to process and which to reject including keeping rejected tasks available in case spare execution time becomes available (from tasks completing earlier than their worst case execution times) or removing guaranteed aperiodic or periodic tasks to provide sufficient time (because the aperiodic request is of greater se- mantic importance). We elaborate on some of these possibilities in section 6, and the methods presented in this paper can be used to support systems in which alternative decision strategies are used.

Each hard deadline aperiodic task can be assigned to execute at any fixed priority level. We assume that if an aperiodic task executes at priority level k , then it has lower priority than any task with priority 1, . . . , k -1 and higher priority thzll any periodic task with priority k , k + 1, . . . , n. Aperiodic task execution at priority level n + 1 is equivalent to background execution.

We conclude this section by listing the specific assumptions under which the analysis in the next two sections is performed. 0 AI: Tasks are ready at the start of their period and do not suspend themselves at any point in time between their activation and their completion. 0 A2: Any subtask can be instantly preempted by any other subtask of higher priority. 0 A$: The (k+l)" instantiation (job) of ri will not begin execution until the kth instantiation of r; has been completed. 0 A4: There is unlimited buffer space at each priority level for the aperiodic tasks.

The subtask model permits the inclusion of many operating system functions and task synchronization using a protocol like priority ceiling emulation. Thus, we need not assume that scheduling overhead, context swapping, task initiation or exiting are negligible, since these can be treated as a part of each task by defining an appropriate subtask. The reader should, however, note that Assumption A5 would appear to limit the scope of the analysis, because most tasks would be initiated and terminated by operating system functions which would normally have execution priority greater than the task priority i . Assumption A5 is being introduced only because it greatly simplifies the schedulability analysis presented in the next section. This assumption can easily be removed using the methods of [2], but considerably more notation would be required.

div.head: Hard Deadline Aperiodic Scheduling
div.p: The hard deadline aperiodic scheduling method proposed in this paper is based on the exact computation of the largest amount of slack available, as in the slack stealing algorithm developed for servicing soft aperiodic tasks in fixed-priority systems [3]. However, there are important differences between the hard and soft aperiodic scheduling problems. These differences include the unattainability of strong optimality and the selection of the priority level used for aperiodic service. These issues are discussed in the following sections and a hard aperiodic scheduling algorithm is then developed.

div.head: Unattainability of Strong Optimality
div.p: Given any on-line scheduling algorithm which guarantees every periodic task deadline, any time spent processing aperiodic tasks which do not eventually meet their deadline is wasted. Hence, only those aperiodic tasks which pass the acceptance test and are guaranteed to meet their deadline should be processed. The acceptance test consists of computing the total processing time that can be made available at a single priority level to service an aperiodic task between its arrival time and its deadline. If the time available is at least as large as the execution time for the aperiodic task, the task is accepted for service; otherwise, it is rejected.

In [3], we considered the soft aperiodic task case, with deadlines Dk = 00. The slack stealing algorithm was proved to be optimal in the class of algorithms which process aperiodic tasks in FIFO order. The definition of optimality proved in [3] is now restated:
We next address the question of optimality.

div.head: Theorem 1 For any periodic task set scheduled by a given fixed priority algorithm and any aperiodic arrival stream processed in FIFO order, the slack stealing algorithm minimizes the response time of every aperiodic task among all scheduling algorithms which meet all periodic task deadlines.
div.p: The conventional view of optimality for hard aperiodic scheduling is that a hard aperiodic scheduling algorithm is optimal if it is guaranteed to schedule any aperiodic task set which can be feasibly scheduled by some other scheduling algorithm; that is, if a hard aperiodic task set is feasible by a hard aperiodic scheduling algorithm, it is also feasible if scheduled by the optimal algorithm. In our view, this defines a very weak sense of optimality because it is limited to the class of hard aperiodic task sets which are schedulable. Since there are many hard aperiodic task sets which fall outside of this restricted class (e.g., fault recovery operations), we are interested in hard aperiodic scheduling problems in which it may be impossible to feasibly schedule the aperiodic tasks by any algorithm. We next provide a definition of strong optimality.

The periodic task set, its phasing and priority assignment are fixed. Consider any sequence of aperiodic jobs J' = { J k , k 2 1). Any scheduling algorithm, call it X, will result in a subset of the aperiodic tasks, Cx (J'), whose deadlines are met. The scheduling problem for hard deadline aperiodic is different from the soft deadline case in that there are aperiodic task sets for which no algorithm can meet all of the aperiodic task deadlines. Thus, any algorithm will create a set of rejected tasks. If the set of aperiodic tasks under consideration is not severely restricted, then no on-line scheduling algorithm can be strongly optimal. To prove this point, suppose we begin with a set of periodic tasks with total utilization U < 1.

We next introduce a single aperiodic task, J1, with a1 = 0 , p l = H x (1-U) and D1 = H. J1 can be completed executing at any priority level, because its computation requirement exactly equals the periodic slack over H. div.head: Deciding on a Service Priority Level
div.p: In the soft aperiodic scheduling case, servicing aperiodic tasks at the highest priority level minimizes a p e riodic response times, as proved in [3]. In the case of hard aperiodic scheduling, there is no value in minimizing aperiodic response times, as long as the aperiodic deadlines are met; that is, if an aperiodic deadline is met by servicing the task at some priority level j , there is no merit in reducing its response time by servicing it at a higher priority level i . Furthermore, we argue that servicing the aperiodic at the higher priority level is not desirable because it results in an unnecessary reduction in the slack available at priority levels i , i + 1,. . . , j -1. This unnecessary reduction in slack jeopardizes the scheduler's ability to service other hard aperiodic tasks. Moreover, servicing hard deadline aperiodics at the lowest possible priority level will maximize the available time at higher levels for short but urgent tasks or soft deadline aperiodics.

In general, hard aperiodic tasks should be scheduled at the lowest priority level possible such that their deadlines are met. To determine such a level, it is recommended that schedulability at the different priority levels be checked, starting with the lowest priority level and moving up until the first priority level is found at which the aperiodic task is schedulable. The ensuing section develops an algorithm for scheduling hard aperiodic tasks at the highest priority level. The case of servicing hard aperiodics at an arbitrary priority level is straightforward [ll] and not covered in this paper.

div.head: Service at Highest Priority
div.p: At any instant in time, say t , , the slack stealer indicates how much aperiodic processing time can be made available immediately, i.e., at the highest priority level. However, it does not indicate how much time can be made available in an arbitrary window of time into the future, [t,, tel. Unlike the scheduling of a soft aperiodic task, a hard aperiodic task must know how much slack can be made available between its arrival and its deadline, so that an acceptance test can be executed.

Scheduling support for slack stealing includes two types of cumulative counters, Ai and T i . Recall that Ai accumulates the aperiodic processing time used and Ti represents the total amount of level-i inactivity observed. These counters are initialized at time 0 and reset at the beginning of each hyperperiod. As a result, every hyperperiod boundary denotes a transition point, requiring that some adjustments be made to the schedulability analysis. The analysis of the other case is not presented here but is similar with minor adjustments needed to account for the fact that counters are reset at hyperperiod boundaries [ l l ] . In general, if an aperiodic task arrives at a time t o and has a deadline at time tb, then the maximum aperiodic processing time available in [to, tb] without violating any deadlines for ri is given by AZ(t,, tb) = min{(tata), Ai(to, tb)}, where Ai(t0,tb) = min{AijJ,Aij(-i + [(at + Dt) -GI} -dl(ta)zi(ta) (11) Observe the similarity of Aj(to,tb) with Equation 7. In scheduling soft aperiodic tasks, the slack stealing algorithm determines, for each task ri, the maximum amount of aperiodic processing time that is available in an interval of time [O,t,], subtracts the time used prior to t o and obtains the aperiodic processing time which can be immediately used at time t o . In scheduling hard aperiodic tasks, the interval of interest is now [to,tb], so the slack stealer computes the maximum amount of aperiodic processing in the interval [O,tb]. Then the aperiodic processing time used prior to t o is subtracted, and the aperiodic processing time available in the interval of interest is obtained. The major difference between the soft and hard aperiodic case is that the maximum cumulative aperiodic processing time for a task ri in both cases is different because the interval over which this time is accumulated changes.

As in the soft aperiodic case, once the maximum cumulative aperiodic processing times are computed for each task, the aperiodic processing time available at the highest priority level is the minimum of these values, as given by A*(to,tb) = mint1 5 i 5 n} AZ(to,tb).

If this is not true, then Jk may be delayed by the execution of higher priority aperiodics in the queue. By the same token, the arrival of Jk may cause lower priority pending aperiodics to be delayed. While the order of complexity of Equation (12) is O(n), its general formulation has a worst-case computational complexity which depends on the maximum number of aperiodic tasks that can be in the aperiodic queue. In theory, this can be unbounded. However, in practice the aperiodic queue has a finite length dictated by the implementation. For the particular case in which the aperiodic tasks are retries of failed periodic tasks with deadlines no greater than their periods, there can never be more than n pending aperiodics at any given time, corresponding to one pending retry per periodic task. As a result, the order of complexity of this general formulation is O(n2) in the worst-case. Our experience indicates that the number of aperiodic tasks in the queue at any instant in time is much smaller than n 80 this worst-case bound is fairly pessimistic. In practice, the computational complexity can be expected to be close to O(n).

div.head: Implementation Requirements
div.p: The implementation of the slack stealing method for servicing hard aperiodic tasks requires the use of all the data structures required to support slack stealing for soft aperiodic service discussed in [3]. These structures include: one level-i inactivity counter per priority level, Zi; one counter for the cumulative aperiodic processing time, AI, since all soft aperiodics are serviced at the highest priority level; one completion status flag per task, where the status can be active, if the task has a pending job, or inactive, if it has no pending job; and a two-dimensional array of slack Values per task, Ai(0,t). The size of the slack array is equal to the sum of the number of jobs for each periodic task within a hyperperiod, or N i , for i = l , . . . , n.

In addition to these structures, the scheduling of hard aperiodic tasks has three more requirements. First, a total of n counters for accumulating used aperiodic service, Ai, for i = 1,. . . , n, are needed because hard aperiodic tasks can be serviced at any priority level. Second, an array containing the latest completion times for all the periodic jobs of the n tasks withing a hyperperiod is needed. The size of this array is the same as that of the slack array. And third, it is necessary to associate one slack variable for each accepted hard aperiodic task in order to ensure that the arrival of future hard aperiodic requests do not cause its guaranteed deadline to be missed. The overall memory requirements of the hard aperiodic scheduling algorithm is summarized in Table 3.

As in the slack stealing algorithm for soft aperiodic service, the main shortcoming of this algorithm for hard aperiodic service is the need for the array of slack values, which has been increased by another array of equal size, namely the completion times array.

Depending on the size of the hyperperiod and the periods of the tasks, these arrays can be relatively large. However, an algorithm which circumvents this shortcoming has been developed and will be presented in a subsequent paper.

div.head: Applications and Extensions
div.p: In this section, we present a series of extensions that are possible with the slack stealing approach presented in this paper. These extensions include many important issues in real-time systems such as the reclamation of unused task execution time, simultaneous service of soft and hard aperiodic scheduling, transient overload and the management of periodic and aperiodic deadlines. These extensions are intended to illustrate that the slack stealing approach provides a flexible framework within which a wide range of possible policies for managing periodic and aperiodic deadlines and soft aperiodic response times can be formulated and implemented.

Reclaiming unused periodic and aperiodic execution time-It is well known that actual task execution times exhibit large variability and may be much less than their worst case execution times [12, 131. The slack stealing method is based on worst case execution times in order to ensure that all deadlines are met under worst case conditions; however, we must have a method of reclaiming any unused execution time. The slack stealing approach offers an especially easy method of reclaiming any unused time. Since every task, whether periodic or aperiodic, is executed at a fixed priority level its execution represents a claim on the slack available at that level. If it does not utilize all of the time claimed, then the excess should be returned to the slack available at that level, say i. A simple way to implement this is to subtract the unused time from the level-k inactivity, zk, i k 5 n. This will make the unused time available to those priority levels.

div.head: Simultaneous service of hard and soft
div.p: aperiodics-This paper has presented the use of the slack stealer for hard aperiodics, and [3] for use on soft aperiodics. Clearly, the method can be extended to service both types of aperiodics. One can partition the slack into two parts, one for hard periodics and the other for soft periodics. A better solution would be to allow the two classes of tasks to draw on the same large pool of slack, thus offering the benefits of resource sharing. The soft aperiodics should be scheduled at the highest priority level, while the hard aperiodics should be scheduled at as low a priority as possible. One should consider putting bounds on the amount of slack that either class can draw over certain periods of time in order to prevent one class from gaining too large a proportion of the available capacity. Such bounds could be adjusted depending on circumstances.

Transient overload-In real-time systems, it is possible that some tasks will exceed their worst case execution times, and a transient overload condition may occur. The slack stealer gives us information at each priority level as to the amount of slack available. Thus one can determine exactly the amount of time a task can overrun its deadline and still not have any other task miss its deadline. Hence, slack stealing provides a new approach to transient overloads, an approach which is far more flexible than period transformations [14].
Modifying periodic deadlines-This paper has assumed that no periodic deadlines may be missed.

This requirement can often be weakened, for example in certain applications, the requirement might be that two consecutive task deadlines should never be missed. For this and similar relaxations of the periodic task deadline requirements, if a hard aperiodic task cannot pass its acceptance test, one can check whether additional slack can be claimed at the desired priority level. This will possibly cause a periodic task to miss a deadline, but this may be preferable to rejecting the aperiodic task.

div.head: Summary
div.p: This paper has presented a slack stealing algorithm for the joint scheduling of hard deadline periodic and aperiodic tasks using fixed priority methods. The methods were presented in a general framework with periodic tasks being composed of serially executed subtasks having possibly distinct execution priorities.

This formulation permits the inclusion of operating system functions and certain synchronization protocols in to the schedulability analysis. The slack stealing approach provides the largest possible amount of time to aperiodic tasks while still guaranteeing the periodic task deadlines. It also provides a framework within which several important generalizations can be carried out including stochastic execution times, transient overloads, simultaneous hard and soft aperiodic service and the relaxation of periodic deadlines.
